chapter.name: Grassroots Democracy -- Part 2: Local Government in Rural Areas

questions.q: True or False? 'Because the Zila Parishad sits at the top of the Panchayati Raj pyramid, it is the tier closest to the people in rural areas.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Gram Panchayat, at the base of the pyramid, is the tier closest to the people in rural areas. The Zila Parishad works at the district level, at the top, farthest from any single village.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the Gram Panchayat at the base is closest to the people; the Zila Parishad is at the district level

questions.q: A villager of Lakshmanpur says: 'The State capital could look after every village itself; there are not that many of us.' Using the chapter's figures (population over 1.4 billion, almost two-thirds of it rural, about 600,000 villages), which reply is correctly worked out?
questions.a: Some 1,550 rural people per village, in about 600,000 villages: too many for one capital
o: Some 1,550 rural people per village, in about 600,000 villages: too many for one capital
Some 2,330 rural people per village, in about 600,000 villages: too many for one capital
Some 780 rural people per village, in about 600,000 villages: too many for one capital
Some 155 rural people per village, so only a few hundred thousand villagers for one capital

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Panchayati Raj system.
1. From the bottom up, its three levels are the village, the block and the district.
2. The Zila Parishad at the district level is also called the Mandal Parishad.
3. Together, its institutions' responsibilities cover almost all aspects of life in the district, from agriculture to cultural activities.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q:
Rampur, a farming village of 180 families, can pay for only one of two works from its own money this year.
Work 1: Extend the canal to the fields at the far end of the village, which it has never reached; 120 families farm those fields.
Work 2: Repair the washed-out stretch of the village's existing road to the bus stop, which all 180 families use, including 25 families whose members work in the town.
The block office has told every village two things: money under the road scheme the chapter names is only for building new all-weather roads, not for repairing existing ones; and any new development project a village puts in its plan can be sent up for funds.
(a) Name the area of responsibility from the chapter's list that each work falls under.
(b) Which work reaches more families, and which affects the earnings of more families? Use the numbers.
Using the block office's message and what the chapter says the block level does with village plans, plan so that both works can get done:
(c) Which work should Rampur pay for itself? Justify.
(d) What should it do with the other work, and how does that work then reach the money it needs?
questions.a: (a) Work 1: management of water resources (agriculture); Work 2: maintenance of roads. (b) The road reaches more families (180 against 120), but the canal affects the earnings of more families (120 farming families against 25 working in town). (c) Pay for the road repair itself. The road work repairs an existing road, so it cannot get money from the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, which promotes the construction of all-weather roads; if Rampur does not pay, nobody will. (d) Put the canal extension into the village's development plan. It is a new development project: the Panchayat Samiti collects the development plans of all Gram Panchayats and presents them at the district or State level, which facilitates the allotment of funds for such projects. So the 120 farming families' canal is not dropped; it goes up the tiers.
s: Part (a): canal under water resources/agriculture, road under maintenance of roads
Part (b): road reaches 180 against 120; canal affects 120 families' earnings against 25
Part (c): pay for the road repair, since the road scheme (PMGSY) funds only new all-weather roads, not repairs
Part (d): send the canal extension up in the development plan, which the Panchayat Samiti collects and presents so funds can be allotted

questions.q: Suppose India's population were split between rural and urban areas in exactly the proportion the chapter gives. Then for every one person living in a town or city, there would be ___ people (write the number) living in villages.

Assertion (A): Lakshmanpur, a village of about 700 people, has its own Panchayat.
Reason (R): Most of the people of Lakshmanpur are farmers who cultivate their lands and rear cows or goats.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A village lists three needs: water for its fields, repair of its main road after heavy rains, and upkeep of its primary school.
(a) Name the area of Panchayati Raj responsibility that each need falls under.
(b) Using your answer to (a), explain why the chapter says these institutions cover 'almost all aspects of life'.
questions.a: (a) Water for fields: management of water resources (agriculture); road: maintenance of roads; school: education. (b) Even one village's three everyday needs fall into three different areas on the list, and the list goes on to housing, health care, social welfare and cultural activities, so very little of daily life lies outside it.
s: Part (a): water resources/agriculture, maintenance of roads, education
Part (b): three needs already span three areas, and the list also covers housing, health, welfare and culture

questions.q: Arun draws Fig. 11.1 for his project. He puts the Zila Parishad at the base of the pyramid, the Panchayat Samiti in the middle and the Gram Panchayat at the top. Which correction should his teacher make?
questions.a: Swap the base and top: Gram Panchayat at the base, Zila Parishad at the top
o: Swap the base and top: Gram Panchayat at the base, Zila Parishad at the top
Move the Panchayat Samiti to the base, as the block is the smallest unit
Keep the base, but replace the Gram Panchayat at the top with the Gram Sabha
Keep the order, but rename the Zila Parishad as the Mandal Parishad

questions.q: Riya says: 'Panchayati Raj simply means the Gram Panchayat of a village; nothing more.' How far is she right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. 'Panchayat' does refer to a village council, and the Gram Panchayat is the base of the system. But the Panchayati Raj system works at three levels, bottom up: the village (Gram Panchayat), the block (Panchayat Samiti) and the district (Zila Parishad), which is why it is called a three-tier system. So the Gram Panchayat is one part of it, not the whole.
s: Verdict: partly right
What is right: Panchayat means a village council and the Gram Panchayat is the base
What she misses: the block and district tiers make it a three-tier system

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Panchayat system described in the chapter.
1. Lakshmanpur has its own Panchayat even though it has only about 200 houses.
2. The chapter calls Panchayati Raj self-government because the State has no authority over these institutions.
3. Panchayats are meant only to carry out schemes sent from the capital, not to promote development.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Compare two ways in which the people of a small village could deal with a broken road, a land dispute and a stolen crop: Way 1, sending every issue to the State or the national capital; Way 2, using the Panchayati Raj system. Analyse why the chapter favours Way 2, using the questions the chapter asks about a village like Lakshmanpur and the roles it gives Panchayats.
questions.a: 1. A village faces many small, everyday issues (a damaged road, a land dispute, stolen crops); the chapter asks whether people can run to the State or national capital for every such issue. 2. Way 1 keeps decisions far away from the people affected, so issues wait. 3. Way 2 brings governance closer to the people, so they can take an active part in decisions, which is why the chapter calls it self-government. 4. Panchayats address local issues and promote development, such as repairing the road. 5. They also make sure that the benefits of government schemes reach the grassroots, so Way 2 is both closer and more effective.
s: Everyday issues are many and small; people cannot run to the capital for each
Weakness of Way 1: decisions far from the village
Way 2 brings governance closer and lets people participate (self-government)
Panchayats address local issues and promote development
Panchayats help government schemes reach the grassroots

questions.q: True or False? 'Since Panchayati Raj is self-government, the villagers decide every matter themselves and do not elect anyone to act for them.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Villagers do take part directly in the Gram Sabha, but the Gram Sabha also elects the members of the Gram Panchayat, who elect the Sarpanch. The chapter says democracy in Panchayati Raj works both through direct participation and through elected representatives.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: villagers also elect representatives (Gram Panchayat, Sarpanch); democracy works both ways

questions.q:
Match each mistaken idea in Column A with the correction the chapter gives in Column B.
Column A: 1. 'The Gram Panchayat is the top tier.'  2. 'Panchayats deal only with farming.'  3. 'Villagers must take every issue to the State capital.'  4. 'Every State's Panchayati Raj is exactly alike.'
Column B: (a) It is the base, the tier closest to the people  (b) Their work runs from roads and schools to health care and cultural activities  (c) Panchayats bring governance close so issues are decided locally  (d) Structure differs a little across States, but the objective is the same

Lakshmanpur has 200 houses and about 700 people.
(a) Another village has about 1,050 people and the same average number of people per house. About how many houses does it have?
(b) A visitor says that a village with fewer than 250 houses is 'too small for a Panchayat'. Using your answer to (a), which of the two villages would he leave without one? Is he right, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) 700 / 200 = 3.5 people per house; 1,050 / 3.5 = 300 houses. (b) He would leave Lakshmanpur (200 houses) without a Panchayat and give one to the other village (300 houses). He is wrong: the chapter says that like every village in India, Lakshmanpur has its own Panchayat, because even a small village has needs (water for fields, its road, its school) and possible disputes over land or stolen crops.
s: Part (a): 3.5 per house, so about 300 houses
Part (b): he would leave out Lakshmanpur (200 < 250), but every village, like Lakshmanpur, has its own Panchayat

questions.q: Sarita says: 'Most people in Lakshmanpur are farmers, so its Panchayat's work is limited to agriculture.' Which fact from the chapter best corrects her?
questions.a: The list also runs to roads, schools, health care and cultural activities
o: The list also runs to roads, schools, health care and cultural activities
Farm matters go only to the Zila Parishad, never to the village Panchayat
Farming is handled by the Patwari, so the Panchayat does none of that work
Agriculture is a State subject that lies outside the Panchayati Raj system

questions.q: Kabir notices that the block-level body is called a Panchayat Samiti in one State and a Mandal Parishad in another. He concludes: 'These must be two different systems, not the same tier.' Test his conclusion using Fig. 11.1.
questions.a: Not correct. Fig. 11.1 gives three names for the same block level: Block Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti and Mandal Parishad. Both bodies sit in the middle of the same three-tier pyramid, between the village level and the district level. Only the name differs; the tier is the same.
s: Verdict: the conclusion is wrong
Fig. 11.1 lists Panchayat Samiti and Mandal Parishad as names of the block level
Both sit between the village and district tiers; only the name differs

questions.q: A State announces a scheme to build toilets in village homes. Lakshmanpur's Panchayat lists the homes without toilets and helps each family apply. Which vital role of Panchayats is it playing?
questions.a: Making sure the benefits of government schemes reach the grassroots
o: Making sure the benefits of government schemes reach the grassroots
Keeping the villagers' land records and the old maps of their fields
Collecting the plans of all the Gram Panchayats of the block together
Electing a head, called the Sarpanch, from among its own members

questions.q:
A villager argues: 'Panchayats cover almost all aspects of village life, so the State government has nothing to do with them.'
(a) Is he right about the State? Answer from the chapter.
(b) Using (a), explain why a Panchayat in one State may look a little different from one in another.
questions.a: (a) No. The chapter says the States have authority over the Panchayati Raj institutions. (b) Because each State has authority over them, their structure and functions differ a little from State to State, though the objective, letting villagers take an active part in managing and developing their area, is the same.
s: Part (a): no, the States have authority over these institutions
Part (b): so structure differs a little by State, while the objective stays the same

questions.q:
Two pupils write essays titled 'Why villages govern themselves'.
Essay P: 'India has about 600,000 villages, and almost two-thirds of its people, about 9 crore, live in rural areas. Leaders in the capital could never look after so many villages.'
Essay Q: 'In a village like Lakshmanpur, people need water for fields, a repaired road and a working school, and may quarrel over land. The people who live there know these needs best and can take part in deciding them.'
(a) Which chapter idea does Essay P's argument rest on?
(b) Which chapter idea does Essay Q's argument rest on?
(c) Correct the population figure in Essay P, using the chapter's numbers.
(d) The prize is for the essay that best explains why the chapter calls Panchayati Raj 'self-government'. Which should win? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The scale of rural India: so many villages and people that distant capitals cannot run each village's affairs. (b) Panchayats bring governance close to the people so they can actively take part in decisions about their own needs. (c) Almost two-thirds of more than 1.4 billion (140 crore) is about 93 crore, not 9 crore. (d) Essay Q. P has data, but it only shows why the capital cannot manage everything; the chapter calls the system self-government because it brings governance close to the people and lets them take part in decision-making, which is Q's point.
s: Part (a): the scale of rural India
Part (b): governance close to the people, who take part in decisions
Part (c): about 93 crore (two-thirds of 140 crore)
Part (d): Essay Q, since self-government means people taking part in their own decisions; P explains only why capitals cannot cope

questions.q: Deepa says: 'A Panchayat that repairs roads and settles quarrels, but never checks whether villagers have received the benefits of government schemes, is not doing everything the chapter expects of it.' Test her claim.
questions.a: Supported. The chapter gives Panchayats three vital roles: addressing local issues, promoting development, and ensuring that the benefits of government schemes reach the grassroots level. Repairing roads and settling quarrels cover local issues (and development), but the third role is left undone, so the Panchayat is doing only part of its job.
s: Verdict: supported
The chapter's three roles: local issues, development, schemes reaching the grassroots
Roads and quarrels cover the first roles; the scheme role is missing

questions.a: (a) Every village has needs (water, roads, its school) and disputes (land, stolen crops), and people cannot run to the State or national capital for each one. (b) The Gram Panchayat. (c) For example: water resources (repairing a canal), roads (filling a washed-out stretch), education (repairing the school), health care (a health camp); others: agriculture, housing, social welfare, cultural activities. (d) Addressing local issues, promoting development and making sure the benefits of government schemes reach the grassroots. (e) It brings governance close to the people so they can take an active part in decision-making.
s: Part (a): needs and disputes that cannot all go to the capital
Part (b): the Gram Panchayat is closest to the people
Part (c): four areas from the chapter's list with fitting examples
Part (d): the three vital roles
Part (e): close to people and their participation make it self-government

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the Gram Sabha, women and men discuss all matters related to their area and take decisions.
Reason (R): In recent years, more and more women have become Sarpanchs.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
In 2026, the Gram Panchayat of Bhojpur chose Kusum as its Sarpanch. Kusum received 7 votes and the other candidate, Harish, received 4. Bhojpur's Gram Sabha has 1,050 members. A shopkeeper says: 'Kusum won with just 7 votes out of 1,050 villagers, so she hardly has the village behind her.'
(a) Who cast the 11 votes in this election?
(b) Which body chose those 11 voters, and how?
(c) Use (a) and (b) to explain why the shopkeeper's '7 out of 1,050' comparison is wrong.
(d) A Bhojpur voter disagrees with the works Kusum has chosen and wants to put her view before the village as a whole, in person. Where can she do this, and why is that the right place?
questions.a: (a) The members of the Gram Panchayat, because each Gram Panchayat elects its own head, the Sarpanch. (b) The Gram Sabha, the adults of the village enrolled as voters, elected them directly. (c) The 1,050 Gram Sabha members did not vote for the Sarpanch at all; they elected the Gram Panchayat members, who then chose the Sarpanch. So the right comparison is 7 out of 11 Gram Panchayat votes. (d) At the Gram Sabha, where women and men of the village discuss all matters related to their area and take decisions; there she can take part directly without going through a representative.
s: Part (a): the Gram Panchayat members
Part (b): the Gram Sabha elected them directly
Part (c): the Gram Sabha never votes for the Sarpanch; the real comparison is 7 of 11
Part (d): the Gram Sabha, where villagers discuss and decide matters directly

questions.q: Three small villages, Amla, Bera and Chuna, share one Gram Sabha. Lata, an adult enrolled as a voter in Chuna, asks whether she may speak and vote on decisions at the Gram Sabha meeting held in Amla. Which answer fits the chapter?
questions.a: Yes: a Gram Sabha can be the adult voters of a group of neighbouring villages
o: Yes: a Gram Sabha can be the adult voters of a group of neighbouring villages
No: each village must hold its own Gram Sabha, so she must wait for Chuna's own meeting
Only if she is one of the members elected to the Gram Panchayat of the area
Only if the Panchayat Secretary, who calls the meetings, adds her name first

questions.q: True or False? 'An adult woman of the village who is enrolled as a voter but holds no seat in the Gram Panchayat can still take part directly in deciding her village's matters.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Being an adult enrolled as a voter makes her a member of the Gram Sabha, and the chapter says that in the Gram Sabha women and men discuss all matters related to their area and take decisions. Village decisions are not left only to the elected Gram Panchayat members.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: as an enrolled adult voter she is in the Gram Sabha, where women and men discuss all matters and take decisions

questions.q: The Gram Sabha of Sonpur has just elected 11 members to its Gram Panchayat. Now a head must be chosen. Ram says all of Sonpur's voters should vote again; Shyam says only the 11 members should vote. Who is right, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Shyam, since each Gram Panchayat elects its own Sarpanch or Pradhan
o: Shyam, since each Gram Panchayat elects its own Sarpanch or Pradhan
Ram, since the Gram Sabha directly elects the Sarpanch as well
Neither, since the Panchayat Samiti appoints each village's Sarpanch
Neither, since the Secretary who calls the meetings names the head

questions.q:
Read the statements about the village level of Panchayati Raj.
1. The members of the Gram Panchayat are elected directly by the Gram Sabha.
2. In the Gram Sabha, only men discuss matters and take decisions.
3. The Panchayat Secretary maintains the villagers' land records.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: One Gram Sabha covers three neighbouring villages. The villages have 210, 340 and 175 adults enrolled as voters, and 160 children between them. The Gram Sabha has ___ members.

At a Gram Sabha meeting in Kheda, a member says: 'Our only job here is to elect the Gram Panchayat; discussing the new well or the market's place is for the Panchayat alone.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: In the Gram Sabha, women and men discuss all matters of the area and decide
o: In the Gram Sabha, women and men discuss all matters of the area and decide
The Gram Sabha may discuss only the matters sent down by the Zila Parishad
The Gram Sabha only elects; matters such as wells are left to the Patwari
The Gram Sabha may discuss matters, but only the Sarpanch may take decisions

questions.q: Differentiate between the Panchayat Secretary and the Patwari by the work each does, and name one record each would keep.
questions.a: The Panchayat Secretary performs administrative functions for the Gram Panchayat, such as calling meetings and maintaining records; for example, the record of a meeting's decisions. The Patwari is an officer who maintains the villagers' land records; for example, a record (or map) of a family's fields, sometimes generations old.
s: Secretary: administrative work such as calling meetings and keeping records, with a fitting record
Patwari: maintains villagers' land records (maps), with a fitting record

questions.q: A student visits two Gram Panchayats. One is assisted by a Patwari; the other is not. She writes that the second one is 'breaking the rules'. Which response matches the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says most, not all, Gram Panchayats have a Patwari's help
o: The chapter says most, not all, Gram Panchayats have a Patwari's help
She is right: every Gram Panchayat must have a Patwari to keep its minutes
She is wrong: Patwaris work only for the Zila Parishad, never in villages
She is right: without a Patwari the Gram Sabha cannot elect its members

questions.q:
The handpump in one lane of Barsoli has been broken for a month.
(a) Which tier of the Panchayati Raj system is closest to the people of Barsoli, and who elects its members?
(b) Using (a), explain why the villagers should raise the handpump with this tier rather than wait for the Zila Parishad.
questions.a: (a) The Gram Panchayat, at the base of the system; its members are elected directly by the Gram Sabha of the village. (b) The Gram Panchayat is the body closest to them and is chosen by the villagers themselves, so it serves their own village and can take up a small local need like one handpump; the Zila Parishad works at the district level, above many villages.
s: Part (a): the Gram Panchayat, elected directly by the Gram Sabha
Part (b): it is close to and chosen by the villagers, while the Zila Parishad is far off at the district level

questions.q:
Read the statements about the village level of Panchayati Raj.
1. A Gram Sabha always belongs to one single village; neighbouring villages never share one.
2. The Sarpanch is elected directly by the Gram Sabha, in the same vote that elects the Gram Panchayat.
3. Besides the Panchayat Secretary, who maintains records, a Gram Panchayat may be assisted by an officer who maintains the villagers' land records.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: Leela says: 'If a village's Gram Sabha meeting lets only the men speak, while the women sit silently at the back, it is not working the way the chapter describes a Gram Sabha.' Is her claim supported? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter describes the Gram Sabha as the adults of a village enrolled as voters, and says that in it women and men discuss all matters related to their area and take decisions. Women are members on the same footing as men, so a meeting that silences them leaves out part of the Gram Sabha from the discussion and the decisions.
s: Verdict: supported
The Gram Sabha is all adults enrolled as voters, women included
In it women and men discuss all matters and take decisions, so silencing women goes against this

questions.q:
Sonpur has 578 adults enrolled as voters, and they elect a Gram Panchayat of 9 members.
(a) How many Gram Sabha members are not on the Gram Panchayat?
(b) Using (a), explain whether these villagers have any part in village decisions after the election.
questions.a: (a) 578 - 9 = 569. (b) Yes. The 569 are still members of the Gram Sabha, where women and men discuss all matters related to their area and take decisions, so most villagers keep taking part directly, not only through the 9 they elected.
s: Part (a): 569
Part (b): yes, they discuss and decide matters in the Gram Sabha

questions.q: Write a short situation (three or four sentences) about an adult who lives in a village but is still NOT a member of its Gram Sabha. Then explain, using the chapter's description, why the person is not a member and what would change that.
questions.a: Sample: Raju, 30, moved to Kheda from a city last year to farm his family's land. He attends Gram Sabha meetings but has never enrolled as a voter in Kheda. He is not a member because the Gram Sabha is made up of adults of the village who are enrolled as voters; living there and being an adult are not enough. If he enrols as a voter in Kheda, he becomes a member and can take part in its decisions and in electing the Gram Panchayat.
s: A situation with an adult who lives in the village but is not enrolled as a voter there
Reason: members are adults enrolled as voters, not just residents
What changes it: enrolling as a voter there

questions.q:
The Patwari of Navgaon keeps a map of the village made 80 years ago. It shows a large pond where houses now stand, a grazing ground that is now fields, and the boundary between two families' fields that are now quarrelling over that boundary.
(a) Whose work is it to keep such records, and what are they called in the chapter?
(b) How could the map help settle the boundary quarrel?
(c) What does the map tell us about Navgaon's past and present?
(d) The Gram Sabha is choosing a place for a new water tank. Suggest one way the map could help this decision, naming the feature on the map you would use.
(e) Which other official of the Gram Panchayat keeps records, and how do those records differ from the Patwari's?
questions.a: (a) The Patwari, who maintains the villagers' land records; in some cases he keeps maps that are generations old. (b) It shows where the boundary between the two fields was recorded long ago, so the families have a record to check instead of only their own claims. (c) It shows how the village has changed: a pond has been filled and built over, and grazing land has become fields, so the old map lets us compare the past with the present. (d) Open: any reasonable use tied to something the map shows earns the mark, for example the old pond shows low land where water once collected, or the old grazing ground and boundaries show which land was common and which belonged to families. (e) The Panchayat Secretary, who performs administrative functions such as calling meetings and maintaining records of the Panchayat's work, not land records.
s: Part (a): the Patwari's land records and old maps
Part (b): the recorded old boundary gives the families a record to check (any wording with this idea)
Part (c): a comparison of past and present (pond built over, grazing land farmed)
Part (d): any reasonable use of the map tied to a feature it shows (old pond, grazing ground, boundaries)
Part (e): the Secretary keeps meeting and administrative records, not land records

questions.q:
In a block with 120 Gram Panchayats, 30 had a woman Sarpanch in 2015 and 48 had one in 2025.
(a) What percentage of the Sarpanchs were women in each year?
(b) Does this fit what the chapter says about women Sarpanchs? Explain using (a).
questions.a: (a) 2015: 30 / 120 = 25%; 2025: 48 / 120 = 40%. (b) Yes. The share rose from 25% to 40%, which fits the chapter's statement that in recent years more and more women have become Sarpanchs.
s: Part (a): 25% and 40%
Part (b): the rise fits 'more and more women have become Sarpanchs'

questions.q: Sohan says: 'The Panchayat Secretary is the most powerful person in the Gram Panchayat, because he calls every meeting and keeps all the records.' Test his claim.
questions.a: Not supported. The chapter says the Gram Panchayat is assisted by a Panchayat Secretary who performs administrative functions such as calling meetings and maintaining records; he helps the Panchayat run, he does not lead it. The head is the Sarpanch or Pradhan, elected by the Gram Panchayat, whose members are elected by the Gram Sabha, where women and men discuss and take decisions.
s: Verdict: not supported
The Secretary only assists with administrative work (meetings, records)
Leadership and decisions lie with the elected Sarpanch, the Gram Panchayat and the Gram Sabha

questions.q:
A newsletter reports: 'The Gram Sabha of Navgaon, which covers Navgaon and the neighbouring villages of Pipri and Sonkhed, met on Sunday. The three villages have 412 adults enrolled as voters; 236 of them came, and about 90 children watched from outside. Women and men discussed two matters. Two families of Pipri disagree about where the boundary between their fields lies. The meeting also decided to build a drinking-water tank near the school, asked that this decision be written down, and asked for a further meeting to be called next month.'
(a) What is the largest number of people who could have taken part in the meeting's decisions? Explain.
(b) The 9 members of the Gram Panchayat were among the 236 who came. How many of those present took part only as ordinary Gram Sabha members, and does the chapter count their discussion as part of decision-making?
(c) Which official will write down the tank decision and call next month's meeting?

Kesar, a drought-hit village of 240 families with poor harvests, wants to follow Hiware Bazar. Its new Sarpanch puts four steps before the Gram Sabha:
Step 1: build small earth bunds and check dams along the slopes and the stream so that rain soaks into the land.
Step 2: collect rainwater from house roofs into tanks and pits.
Step 3: plant 1,08,000 saplings on bare land over 3 years.
Step 4: deepen every borewell by 100 feet so that the pumps reach water again.
(a) Three of the steps follow the model Popatrao Pawar applied. Name the model and match each of those three steps to one of its parts.
(b) Explain why Step 4 does not belong with the other three, using what the chapter says those measures did for Hiware Bazar's groundwater.
(c) If the 240 families share Step 3 equally, how many saplings must each family plant per year? Write Kesar's total in lakhs, the unit the chapter uses for Hiware Bazar's trees.
(d) After the first monsoon the wells are still low, and a ward member says, 'The plan has failed; drop it.' Judge his remark, using how long Hiware Bazar's change took.
questions.a: (a) Anna Hazare's model: Step 1 is watershed conservation, Step 2 is rainwater harvesting, Step 3 is massive tree planting. (b) The chapter says these measures all contributed to the recharge of groundwater: they put water back into the ground. Deepening borewells only draws out the water already there, from deeper down; it adds nothing back, so it is not one of the model's parts and works the other way. (c) 1,08,000 / 240 = 450 saplings per family; 450 / 3 = 150 per family per year. The total is 1.08 lakh. (d) He judges too soon. Hiware Bazar became green and prosperous 'in a few years', not in one season, because recharging groundwater takes time, and it needed the villagers' collaboration throughout. One monsoon is too early to call the plan a failure.
s: Part (a): Anna Hazare's model; bunds and check dams = watershed conservation, roof water = rainwater harvesting, saplings = tree planting
Part (b): the three measures recharge groundwater; deepening borewells only draws water out
Part (c): 150 saplings per family per year; 1.08 lakh in all
Part (d): too soon to judge, since Hiware Bazar's change took a few years

Rajasthan: children's elections and a Cabinet overseeing school management
Judgement: the Children's Parliament gave children the largest part
Reason: children voted, campaigned and oversaw work, unlike Sikkim

questions.q: A Gram Panchayat has just been declared child-friendly. Write three things it might have done, each based on a different example from the chapter, and name the example each comes from.
questions.a: Sample: (1) It built a compound wall round the village school and a kitchen for hygienically cooked mid-day meals (Sangkhu Radhu Khandu, Sikkim). (2) It set up a Bal Panchayat whose members convince parents to send working children back to school and not to marry off girls who should be studying (Maharashtra's Bal Panchayats). (3) It helped children hold elections with voter ID cards and form a Cabinet to oversee school matters (Rajasthan's Children's Parliament).
s: An action based on Sangkhu Radhu Khandu, named
An action based on Maharashtra's Bal Panchayats, named
An action based on the Children's Parliament, named

questions.q:
A school in rural Rajasthan runs elections modelled on the Children's Parliament. There are 136 children: 120 aged 8 to 14, 10 aged 15 or 16 and 6 aged 6 or 7. As in the Children's Parliament, only children in its age band, 8 to 14, may vote. On election day, 90 of those allowed to vote do so. The new Cabinet can take up only one plan this term:
Plan 1: press for repairs to the girls' toilets, which the Gram Panchayat has already put in this year's plan.
Plan 2: start an evening reading class for 30 children of the village who work by day and do not attend school; nobody else has offered to run it.
(a) How many voter ID cards should be issued? Explain.
(b) What percentage of those allowed to vote did vote?
(c) Name the chapter's issue that each plan belongs to.
(d) Which plan should the Cabinet choose? Justify using how the Children's Parliament itself worked.
questions.a: (a) 120: only children aged 8 to 14 may vote, so the 10 older and 6 younger children are left out (136 - 16 = 120). (b) 90 / 120 = 75%. (c) Plan 1: sanitation; Plan 2: access to education. (d) Plan 2. Both fit issues the children addressed, but the toilets are already in the Gram Panchayat's plan, while the 30 working children have no one else. The Children's Parliament itself reached underprivileged children through night schools, so an evening class follows its own method.
s: Part (a): 120 cards, ages 8 to 14 only
Part (b): 75%
Part (c): sanitation and access to education
Part (d): Plan 2, as the toilets are already planned and night schooling is how the Parliament reached working children

questions.q: Write a letter to the Sarpanch of your village proposing a Bal Panchayat. The letter must (a) say what a Bal Panchayat is for, (b) suggest how its members could be chosen, borrowing from the Children's Parliament, (c) name two issues it would take up, each linked to an example in the chapter, (d) say what role you expect the village elders to play, and (e) mention one award or recognition from the chapter to show that such forums work.
questions.a: A good letter: (a) gives children a chance to express ideas and opinions on matters that concern their wellbeing, since Panchayats should listen to everyone, children included; (b) holds an election with voter ID cards and campaigning, as the Children's Parliament did, with children of a fixed age range; (c) e.g. bringing working children back to school and stopping child marriages (Maharashtra's Bal Panchayats), and a safer school or hygienic mid-day meals (Sangkhu Radhu Khandu); (d) the elders listen and try to find solutions to the children's concerns; (e) the Children's Parliament's World's Children's Honorary Award in 2001, or Sangkhu Radhu Khandu being declared child-friendly.
s: Part (a): purpose: children express views on their wellbeing; Panchayats listen to all
Part (b): election method borrowed from the Children's Parliament
Part (c): two issues, each linked to a chapter example
Part (d): elders try to find solutions to children's concerns
Part (e): a recognition named in the chapter

questions.q:
(a) The Children's Parliament received the World's Children's Honorary Award in 2001. How many years before 2026 was that?
(b) In a village school, children of one community are made to sit apart from the others at the mid-day meal. A child speaks out and gets the custom stopped. Name what the chapter says the initiative enabled children to do that this child is doing, and which of the issues the children addressed it belongs to.
questions.a: (a) 2026 - 2001 = 25 years. (b) The child is challenging a societal norm (and advocating for change), which the chapter says the initiative enabled children to do. It belongs to social equality, one of the issues the children addressed, alongside access to education and sanitation.
s: Part (a): 25 years
Part (b): challenging societal norms, under the issue of social equality

questions.q: A Zila Parishad has 36 seats. Under the provision for women that the chapter describes, ___ of these seats are reserved for women.

Five Gram Panchayats of Sonpur block have drawn up their development plans for the year:
GP A: 4 km of all-weather road; the village has no all-weather road at all.
GP B: 6 km of all-weather road; the village already has one all-weather road.
GP C: a compound wall for its school.
GP D: 3 km of all-weather road; the village has no all-weather road at all.
GP E: 5 km of all-weather road; the village already has one all-weather road.
(a) Which body collects these plans, and to which level does it present them?
(b) Which government scheme named in the chapter could fund the road plans?
(c) Why should GP C's plan go up along with the road plans, even though it is not a road?
(d) Road funds this year cover only 10 km, for whole requests only. The block's rule is that villages with no all-weather road at all come first, and other requests are funded only if a whole request still fits in what is left. One member wants A and B, which uses all 10 km; another wants A and D. Which requests does the rule fund, how many km are left, and can any other request use them? Show the working.
questions.a: (a) The Panchayat Samiti of the block collects the plans of all its Gram Panchayats, puts them together and presents them at the district level (the Zila Parishad) or the State level. (b) The Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, which promotes all-weather roads in rural areas. (c) The Samiti coordinates matters across all its Gram Panchayats by collecting the plans of every one of them, which helps funds to be allotted for development projects in general, not only for roads. (d) Under the rule, A and D come first, as both have no all-weather road: 4 + 3 = 7 km, leaving 10 - 7 = 3 km. B needs 6 km and E needs 5 km, both more than 3, so no other whole request fits and 3 km stay unused this year. The A-and-B pair would use all 10 km, but it breaks the rule by serving B, which already has a road, while D, which has none, waits.
s: Part (a): the Panchayat Samiti, presenting at the district (or State) level
Part (b): the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana
Part (c): the Samiti collects plans from all Gram Panchayats for all development projects
Part (d): A and D under the rule (4 + 3 = 7 km); 3 km left, too little for B (6) or E (5)

questions.q: In one village, the families of a poor hamlet rarely speak at meetings, and their needs never get into the village's plans. Which provision described in the chapter is meant for exactly this problem?
questions.a: Special rules so that disadvantaged sections can make their needs heard

Read the statements about the block and district levels.

questions.q: Sunil says: 'The Panchayat Samiti does not take the place of the Gram Panchayats under it. It links them and coordinates their work.' Is his claim supported by the chapter? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter calls the Panchayat Samiti the link between the Gram Panchayat and the Zila Parishad, so the Gram Panchayats remain at the village level below it. It says the Samitis coordinate matters across Gram Panchayats, for instance by collecting development plans from all of them and putting them together for the district or State level. That is linking and coordinating, not replacing.

The Samiti is the link between the Gram Panchayat and Zila Parishad; the Gram Panchayats stay
It coordinates by collecting and combining all the Gram Panchayats' plans

questions.q: Your class will interview a member of the Panchayat Samiti. Which question shows that you understand the Samiti's own role, as the chapter describes it?

questions.q:
A district has six blocks with 15, 22, 18, 25, 20 and 16 Gram Panchayats.
(a) How many Gram Panchayats does the district have in all?
(b) Using (a), explain how the Panchayat Samitis make the district level's work manageable.
questions.a: (a) 15 + 22 + 18 + 25 + 20 + 16 = 116. (b) Each Panchayat Samiti collects the development plans of all the Gram Panchayats in its block and puts them together, so the district level receives 6 combined block plans instead of 116 separate village plans; the Samiti is the link between the Gram Panchayats and the Zila Parishad.
s: Part (a): 116 Gram Panchayats
Part (b): 6 Samitis combine the plans, so the district deals with 6 sets, not 116

questions.q: A student designing a poster on the Panchayati Raj system has four statements on it. Which one must she remove, because the chapter contradicts it?
questions.a: Seats are reserved for women only in Gram Panchayats
o: Seats are reserved for women only in Gram Panchayats
One-third of the seats can be reserved for women
Women's reservation applies at all three tiers
Special rules help disadvantaged sections to be heard

questions.q: Differentiate between the Gram Panchayat and the Panchayat Samiti, by the level each works at and the main work the chapter gives each.
questions.a: The Gram Panchayat works at the village level, closest to the people; its members are elected directly by the Gram Sabha, and it takes up the village's own matters. The Panchayat Samiti works at the block level, above many villages; it is the link to the Zila Parishad and coordinates matters across Gram Panchayats, such as collecting all their development plans and putting them together.
s: Gram Panchayat: village level, closest to the people, elected by the Gram Sabha
Panchayat Samiti: block level, links to the Zila Parishad and coordinates the Gram Panchayats' plans

questions.q: Four Gram Panchayats send proposals with their development plans. Which one fits most directly the government scheme the chapter names, as the chapter describes its purpose?
questions.a: Building an all-weather road to a hamlet that is cut off in the rains
o: Building an all-weather road to a hamlet that is cut off in the rains
Filling the potholes on the village's existing all-weather road
A compound wall to keep pupils safe from the highway beside the school
Rainwater-harvesting pits so that a drought-hit village's wells refill

questions.q: Akash's chart puts the Panchayat Samiti at the very top of the pyramid, above the Zila Parishad. Show, using the chapter's description of the Panchayat Samiti, that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says the Panchayat Samiti, at the block level, is the link between the Gram Panchayat and the Zila Parishad. A link between two bodies must lie between them, so the Samiti sits above the village-level Gram Panchayat and below the district-level Zila Parishad. Fig. 11.1 agrees: village, then block, then district from the bottom up. So the Zila Parishad, not the Samiti, is at the top.
s: The Samiti is described as the link between the Gram Panchayat and the Zila Parishad
A link must sit between the two, at the block level
So the order is village, block, district; the Zila Parishad is at the top

questions.q: A Panchayat Samiti in one State has 25 members; one in another State has 40 and includes local members of the State Legislative Assembly. A student concludes that one of them cannot really be a Panchayat Samiti. Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: Make-up can differ by State; the role stays the same
o: Make-up can differ by State; the role stays the same
Only the larger body is a true Samiti, as it has more members
A body with Assembly members must be a Zila Parishad
Every Samiti must have the same 25 members across India

questions.q: Mohan says: 'The Zila Parishad is just one very big Gram Panchayat, elected by a single Gram Sabha made up of all the adults of the district.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Not supported. A Gram Sabha is the adult voters of a village or a group of neighbouring villages, not of a whole district. The Zila Parishad is a separate body at the district level, the top tier, above the Panchayat Samiti. Its members are elected by the local people, but it may also have other members, such as Sarpanchs of the villages in the area and local members of the State Legislative Assembly, which the chapter does not describe for a Gram Panchayat.
s: Verdict: not supported
A Gram Sabha covers a village or neighbouring villages, not a district
The Zila Parishad is a separate district-level tier that may include Sarpanchs and MLAs

questions.q:
(a) A visitor says: 'The Zila Parishad collects the development plans directly from every Gram Panchayat.' Correct him.
(b) Give one thing the chapter says is common to the Panchayat Samiti and the Zila Parishad.
questions.a: (a) It is the Panchayat Samiti, at the block level, that collects the development plans from all its Gram Panchayats, puts them together and presents them at the district or State level; the Samiti is the link between the Gram Panchayat and the Zila Parishad. (b) Any one: their members are elected by the local people; they may also have other members such as Sarpanchs of the area and local members of the State Legislative Assembly; one-third of seats can be reserved for women.
s: Part (a): the Samiti collects and combines the plans and presents them upward
Part (b): one shared feature (elected by local people, other members, or reservation for women)

questions.q:
Students of a village school find it hard to cross the highway beside their school. Their parents raise it at the Gram Sabha, and the Gram Panchayat puts a footbridge into its development plan.
(a) Which body collects this plan, and what does it do with it?
(b) Why does this step matter for getting the footbridge built?
(c) Name one thing the students themselves can do, using a forum the chapter describes.
questions.a: (a) The Panchayat Samiti of the block; it collects the development plans of all the Gram Panchayats, puts them together and presents them at the district or State level. (b) The chapter says this facilitates the allotment of funds for such development projects. (c) Raise the problem in a Bal Sabha or Bal Panchayat, where children express their concerns and village elders try to find solutions (or, like Maharashtra's Bal Panchayat members, speak to adults themselves).
s: Part (a): the Panchayat Samiti collects, combines and presents the plans
Part (b): this helps funds to be allotted
Part (c): raise it in a Bal Sabha or Bal Panchayat

questions.q:
(a) A Panchayat Samiti has 34 members: 22 elected by the local people, 2 local members of the State Legislative Assembly, and the rest Sarpanchs of the villages in the area. How many Sarpanchs sit in it?
(b) Suggest why having the Sarpanchs of the area as members could help a Panchayat Samiti do the work the chapter gives it.
questions.a: (a) 34 - 22 - 2 = 10 Sarpanchs. (b) The Samiti's work is to coordinate across Gram Panchayats and put together their development plans; Sarpanchs head those Gram Panchayats, so they can bring their villages' plans and needs straight to the Samiti.
s: Part (a): 10 Sarpanchs
Part (b): Sarpanchs bring their Gram Panchayats' plans to a body that coordinates them

questions.q: The chapter asks: 'Why do you think it is important for the government to pay more attention to the needs and problems of the disadvantaged sections of society?' Answer it by covering: (a) the two provisions the chapter describes at all three levels; (b) what can happen to a village plan if some groups are never heard; (c) an example from the chapter of a group that was once kept out of village decisions and was brought in; (d) the objective that the chapter says all Panchayati Raj institutions share; (e) a judgement linking (b) and (d).
questions.a: (a) Special rules so that disadvantaged sections can make their needs and problems heard, and the reservation of one-third of the seats for women. (b) In the Gram Sabha, women and men discuss all matters and take decisions, and the village's development plan is what the Panchayat Samiti later collects and presents for funds; if some groups are never heard, their needs can be missing from those decisions and so from the plans that go up for funds. (c) Women in Khankhandvi: Vandana Maida defied patriarchal norms and convinced women to attend the Sabha meetings. (d) To enable villagers to take an active part in the management and development of their villages and local area. (e) If some groups are unheard, the system cannot meet that objective for all villagers, so extra attention to them is needed for the plans to serve everyone.
s: Part (a): special rules for disadvantaged sections and one-third seats for women
Part (b): unheard groups' needs can be missing from the decisions and the plans sent up for funds
Part (c): women brought into the Sabha by Vandana Maida
Part (d): villagers taking an active part in managing and developing their area
Part (e): the objective needs everyone heard, so extra attention is justified

questions.q:
Two States run their Panchayat Samitis differently:
State X: members elected by the local people, plus the Sarpanchs of the area. One-third of the seats are reserved for women.
State Y: members elected by the local people, plus the Sarpanchs of the area and local members of the State Legislative Assembly. One-third of the seats are reserved for women.
(a) A Panchayat Samiti in State X has 24 seats. How many are reserved for women?
(b) A visitor says State Y's body 'cannot be a Panchayat Samiti, because MLAs sit in it'. Is he right? Explain.
(c) Why are X and Y allowed to differ, and what does the chapter say stays the same in both? Judge whether the difference matters.
questions.a: (a) 24 / 3 = 8 seats. (b) No: the chapter says these bodies may have other members such as Sarpanchs and local members of the State Legislative Assembly, and that the composition of Panchayat Samitis differs from State to State. (c) The States have authority over the Panchayati Raj institutions, so their structure differs a little. What stays the same is the role of strengthening the participation of local people and the objective of letting villagers take an active part in managing and developing their area; since both keep that, and both reserve one-third of seats for women, the difference in membership does not change the purpose.
s: Part (a): 8 seats
Part (b): wrong, as MLAs may be members and composition differs by State
Part (c): States have authority; the role and objective stay the same, so the difference does not change the purpose

questions.q:
A State committee discusses three proposals for its Panchayati Raj system:
Proposal 1: 'Abolish the Panchayat Samitis; let each Gram Panchayat deal directly with the Zila Parishad.'
Proposal 2: 'Fill every Panchayat Samiti seat with the Sarpanchs of the block, so no separate election by the local people is needed.'
Proposal 3: 'Copy every rule of the neighbouring State, so that the two systems are identical.'
Evaluate each proposal against the chapter, and then give your overall advice.
questions.a: Proposal 1: weak. The Samiti is the link between the Gram Panchayat and the Zila Parishad; it coordinates matters across Gram Panchayats by collecting their development plans and putting them together, which facilitates the allotment of funds. Without it the district would receive scattered plans from every village. Proposal 2: goes against the chapter, which says the members of these institutions are elected by the local people; Sarpanchs may sit as other members, but they do not replace the elected ones. Proposal 3: allowed but not needed: States have authority over these institutions, so structures may differ a little; what must stay the same is the objective of villagers taking an active part in managing and developing their area. Overall: reject 1 and 2; 3 is a choice for the State, as long as the objective is kept.
s: Proposal 1: rejected, as the Samiti links and coordinates the Gram Panchayats' plans
Proposal 1: what would be lost (combining plans for funds)
Proposal 2: rejected, as Samiti members are elected by the local people; Sarpanchs only may be added
Proposal 3: allowed, as States have authority, but not required; the objective must stay
Overall advice consistent with the three verdicts

questions.q:
The chapter says the Arthashastra was written 'some 2,300 years ago'.
(a) Taking the present year as 2026, in which century BCE was it written?
(b) Using (a), about how many centuries before today's Panchayati Raj was its village-upward plan described, and why does the chapter call this 'amazing'?
questions.a: (a) 2,300 - 2,026 = 274, so it was written in about the 270s BCE, that is, the 3rd century BCE (approximate, as the chapter says 'some'). (b) About 23 centuries (2,300 years) earlier. Kautilya already described administration built up from the village to larger units and the regional capital, much like today's village-block-district tiers; an idea that old being so close to today's is what the chapter finds amazing.
s: Part (a): the 3rd century BCE (about 270s BCE)
Part (b): about 23 centuries earlier, yet a village-upward structure like today's

questions.q:
A kingdom of 1,600 villages is organised exactly as the Arthashastra passage in the chapter says. Match each unit with the number of such units the kingdom needs.
Column A: 1. sangrahana  2. karvatika  3. dronamukha  4. sthaniya
Column B: (a) 160  (b) 16  (c) 4  (d) 2
True or False? 'The administrative structure described in the Arthashastra, like today's Panchayati Raj, has exactly three levels.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The Arthashastra passage names four categories: a sangrahana for every 10 villages, a karvatika for every 100, a dronamukha for every 400 and a sthaniya for every 800. Today's Panchayati Raj is the one with three tiers: village, block and district.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the Arthashastra has four categories (10, 100, 400, 800 villages); Panchayati Raj has three tiers

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the Arthashastra's plan, the district headquarters served a smaller group of villages than a dronamukha did.
Reason (R): The passage names the karvatika as the district headquarters and sets one for every 100 villages, against one dronamukha for every 400.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A classmate says, 'Our Panchayati Raj system was simply copied from Kautilya's Arthashastra.' Which reply fits what the chapter says?
questions.a: The chapter only notes a similar structure long ago
o: The chapter only notes a similar structure long ago
Yes: the Gram Panchayat is Kautilya's own sangrahana
No: the Arthashastra dealt with cities, not villages
Yes: the chapter says the tiers are Kautilya's units

questions.q: An elderly villager says: 'Panchayati Raj is a new idea with no roots in India's past.' Which point from the chapter answers him most directly?
questions.a: The Arthashastra, some 2,300 years old, describes a village-upward structure
o: The Arthashastra, some 2,300 years old, describes a village-upward structure
Anna Hazare's model of rainwater harvesting was applied in Hiware Bazar
Bunker Roy's Barefoot College gave rise to Rajasthan's Children's Parliament
Gandhi's line says that the real India lives in its villages, not its cities

questions.q:
A historian builds a model kingdom organised exactly as the Arthashastra passage in the chapter describes. The model has 6 sthaniyas and nothing outside them.
(a) How many villages does the model kingdom have?
(b) How many dronamukhas and how many karvatikas does it need?
(c) Work backwards: how many sangrahanas would be set up for the 100 villages that one karvatika serves?
(d) A student wants to label the karvatikas 'Kautilya's Zila Parishads'. Using the passage and the chapter, judge whether the label is fair: give one way it fits and one way it does not.
questions.a: (a) 6 x 800 = 4,800 villages. (b) 4,800 / 400 = 12 dronamukhas and 4,800 / 100 = 48 karvatikas. (c) 100 / 10 = 10 sangrahanas. (d) Partly fair. It fits because the passage itself calls the karvatika a district headquarters, and the Zila Parishad works at the district level. It does not fit exactly because the king establishes a karvatika for every 100 villages, while the Zila Parishad's members are elected by the local people; the chapter calls the two structures similar, not the same.
s: Part (a): 4,800 villages
Part (b): 12 dronamukhas and 48 karvatikas
Part (c): 10 sangrahanas
Part (d): partly fair: both are district-level, but one is set up by the king, the other elected

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Arthashastra as the chapter describes it.
1. Because it explains how to conduct war, it cannot be called a text of governance.
2. Its plan starts from the village and builds up to the regional capital.
3. In its plan, the villagers of every 10 villages elect their own sangrahana.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A museum label reads: 'The Arthashastra, a text of governance by Chanakya, about 2,300 years old.' A visitor objects that the chapter names the author as Kautilya. Who is right?
questions.a: The label is fine: Kautilya was later known as Chanakya
o: The label is fine: Kautilya was later known as Chanakya
The visitor: Chanakya was the king for whom Kautilya wrote
The visitor: Chanakya wrote a later commentary, not the text
The label is fine only if 'governance' becomes 'war'

questions.q: Divya claims: 'Long before Panchayati Raj, the Arthashastra too organised villages into bigger and bigger units for governing them.' Is her claim supported by the chapter? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. The Arthashastra explains how an administrative structure should be put in place from the village to the regional capital: a sangrahana for every 10 villages, a karvatika for every 100, a dronamukha for every 400 and a sthaniya for every 800. Each unit covers more villages than the one before. The chapter itself calls it amazing that a similar structure was thought of so long ago, some 2,300 years ago, close to today's village-block-district system.
s: Verdict: supported
Evidence: units for 10, 100, 400 and 800 villages, from village to regional capital
The chapter notes this is similar to today's tiers, thought of about 2,300 years ago

questions.q: The chapter asks: 'Is it not amazing that a similar structure was thought of so long ago?' What likeness does 'similar' refer to?
questions.a: Both build administration up from villages to larger units
o: Both build administration up from villages to larger units
Both have exactly three levels from the village to the top
Both let the villagers elect the members at every level
Both use the same names for their levels, in older forms

questions.q:
(a) Which unit does the Arthashastra passage call the 'district headquarters', and for how many villages?
(b) A student labels the dronamukha as the district headquarters, saying 'it covers more villages, so it must be the district'. Correct her using the passage.
questions.a: (a) The karvatika, one for every 100 villages. (b) The passage gives the name 'district headquarters' to the karvatika, not the dronamukha. The dronamukha is the unit for every 400 villages, and the passage gives it no such label; the next named one, the sthaniya for 800 villages, is the provincial headquarters.
s: Part (a): the karvatika, for every 100 villages
Part (b): the passage calls the karvatika the district headquarters; the dronamukha is the 400-village unit with no such label

questions.q: Kunal claims: 'Kautilya's sangrahana was exactly the same thing as today's Gram Panchayat.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Not supported. The passage describes a sangrahana as a sub-district headquarters that the king shall establish for every 10 villages. Today's Gram Panchayat is a village council whose members are elected directly by the Gram Sabha, the adult voters of a village or a group of neighbouring villages. One is set up from above by the king, the other is chosen by the people; the chapter calls the two structures similar, not the same.
s: Verdict: not supported
Sangrahana: a sub-district headquarters the king establishes for every 10 villages
Gram Panchayat: elected by the Gram Sabha; the chapter says only 'similar'

questions.q: A pupil wants one phrase from the Arthashastra passage as evidence that its units were set up from above, not chosen by villagers. Which phrase should she quote?
questions.a: 'The king shall establish a sangrahana...'
o: 'The king shall establish a sangrahana...'
'...for every 10 villages'
'...a karvatika (district headquarters)'
'...a sthaniya (provincial headquarters) for every 800 villages'

questions.q:
The chapter asks: 'In today's language, what are the names we would give these four categories?'
(a) Give today's names for the sangrahana and the sthaniya, using the passage's own descriptions.
(b) The passage gives no modern label for the dronamukha. Suggest one, and justify it from the number of villages it covers.
questions.a: (a) Sangrahana: a sub-district headquarters; sthaniya: a provincial headquarters. (b) For example, a 'division' or 'regional headquarters': it serves 400 villages, more than a karvatika (district headquarters, 100 villages) and fewer than a sthaniya (province, 800 villages), so its name must sit between district and province.
s: Part (a): sub-district headquarters and provincial headquarters
Part (b): a name between district and province, justified by 400 lying between 100 and 800

questions.q: Compare the administrative structure in the Arthashastra with today's Panchayati Raj system, and analyse how alike they really are. Cover: (a) how many levels each has; (b) how each level is defined; (c) who sets up or chooses the units; (d) what each structure is part of or aims at; and (e) the one likeness the chapter itself points out.
questions.a: (a) The Arthashastra names four categories (sangrahana, karvatika, dronamukha, sthaniya); Panchayati Raj has three tiers. (b) Kautilya defines units by counts of villages: 10, 100, 400 and 800; Panchayati Raj uses the village, the block and the district. (c) In the Arthashastra the king shall establish the units; in Panchayati Raj, members are elected: the Gram Sabha elects the Gram Panchayat, and local people elect the members of the higher bodies. (d) The Arthashastra is a text on how a king should run a state, its economy and war; Panchayati Raj is a form of self-government that lets villagers take an active part in managing and developing their area. (e) Both build administration up from the village to bigger units, which the chapter calls amazing for an idea some 2,300 years old.
s: Part (a): four categories against three tiers
Part (b): counts of villages against village, block and district
Part (c): set up by the king against elected by the people
Part (d): a king's statecraft against self-government
Part (e): both build up from the village, a similar structure

questions.q: True or False? 'The Arthashastra was written to guide a king, so it says nothing about how villages were to be organised.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. It does describe the duties of the ruler and how to conduct war, but the chapter says Kautilya also explains how a whole administrative structure should be put in place from the village to the regional capital, for example a sangrahana for every 10 villages.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it also sets out an administrative structure from the village up to the regional capital

questions.q:
A pupil draws Kautilya's plan as a pyramid like Fig. 11.1, one layer for each unit.
(a) Which unit goes at the base and which at the top?
(b) Give two ways in which her pyramid would be labelled differently from Fig. 11.1.
questions.a: (a) The sangrahana (for every 10 villages) at the base and the sthaniya (for every 800 villages, the provincial headquarters) at the top. (b) It has four layers, not three; and its layers are defined by numbers of villages (10, 100, 400, 800), while Fig. 11.1 uses levels named village, block and district.
s: Part (a): sangrahana at the base, sthaniya at the top
Part (b): four layers not three, and defined by village counts rather than village, block and district

questions.q:
A newsletter from Sonpur village reads: 'Last year we elected our Gram Panchayat. This spring, women and men met in the Gram Sabha and agreed that a check dam was needed. The Gram Panchayat put the check dam into its development plan, and the plan went to the Panchayat Samiti with the plans of the other villages of the block. A year later, the plans have been presented at the district level, but the funds have not yet come.'
(a) Which sentence shows direct participation?
(b) Which sentence shows democracy through elected representatives?
(c) One villager says the delay proves that Panchayati Raj gives Sonpur no self-governance; another says Sonpur's self-governance is real but only partial. Judge between them, using the newsletter and the chapter's summary.
questions.a: (a) 'Women and men met in the Gram Sabha and agreed that a check dam was needed.' (b) 'Last year we elected our Gram Panchayat' (and the Gram Panchayat then put the dam into its plan). (c) The second villager is right. Sonpur's people did decide and plan for themselves, through the Gram Sabha and their elected Gram Panchayat, so self-governance is real and the first villager is wrong. But the plan had to go to the Panchayat Samiti, which presents plans at the district or State level, and that presenting and deciding at the higher levels is what facilitates the allotment of funds, so part of the outcome rests with the higher tiers. That is what the chapter means by 'a measure of self-governance': real, but not complete.
s: Part (a): the Gram Sabha sentence
Part (b): electing the Gram Panchayat
Part (c): partial self-governance: villagers decided and planned, but funds depend on the higher tiers ('a measure of')

questions.q: Write a rule in the style of the Arthashastra passage, but for today's three tiers (for example, 'There shall be a ___ for every ___ ...'). Then explain two ways in which your rule does not match how Panchayati Raj actually works, according to the chapter.
questions.a: Sample rule: 'The State shall establish a Gram Panchayat for every village or group of neighbouring villages, a Panchayat Samiti for every block and a Zila Parishad for every district.' Differences: (1) the rule says the State 'shall establish' the bodies, but the chapter says their members are elected by the people, the Gram Panchayat directly by the Gram Sabha; (2) one fixed rule for the whole country misses that the structure and functions differ a little from State to State, because the States have authority over these institutions.
s: A rule naming the three tiers in the passage's style
Difference 1: members are elected by the people, not set up from above
Difference 2: structure differs a little by State, as States have authority

questions.q: 'The Panchayati Raj institutions give people in rural areas a measure of self-governance.' Justify this statement by drawing one piece of evidence from each of these parts of the chapter: (a) the Gram Sabha; (b) the Gram Panchayat and its head; (c) an exemplary Sarpanch; (d) a child-friendly initiative; (e) the Panchayat Samiti.
questions.a: (a) In the Gram Sabha, the adults enrolled as voters, women and men discuss all matters of their area and take decisions themselves. (b) The Gram Sabha directly elects the Gram Panchayat, which elects its own head, the Sarpanch or Pradhan, so villagers choose who governs them. (c) For example, Popatrao Pawar, as Sarpanch, worked with the villagers on rainwater harvesting and tree planting until drought-hit Hiware Bazar became green and prosperous: the village solved its own problem. (d) For example, Maharashtra's Bal Panchayats, where children convinced parents to send their wards back to school: even children take part. (e) The Panchayat Samiti collects the development plans of all the Gram Panchayats and puts them together for the district or State, so villages shape the plans that get funds.
s: Part (a): the Gram Sabha discusses and decides
Part (b): villagers elect the Gram Panchayat, which elects the Sarpanch
Part (c): an exemplary Sarpanch's village solving its own problem
Part (d): a child-friendly initiative where children take part
Part (e): the Samiti carries the villages' own plans upwards
